title: Systemd Unit Failures
exclusions: Covers failures reported by the host's system systemd manager in two explicit forms: a unit observed with `ActiveState=failed` by the documented `systemctl` collector, and a system-manager start job carrying systemd's `SD_MESSAGE_UNIT_FAILED` journal message ID. It does not treat `inactive`, `not-found`, `masked`, a skipped condition, an application log containing the word "error", or every priority-3 journal record as a unit failure. The message ID `be02cf6855d2428ba40df7e9d022f03d` means a start job failed; systemd's source explicitly warns that it is not a universal unit-failed event. A short runtime failure that auto-recovers between 60-second state polls and does not produce that start-job message can therefore be missed. User managers (`systemctl --user`), containers with a separate manager namespace, remote machines selected with `systemctl --host`/`--machine`, unloaded units, dependency root-cause analysis, service-level health, restart-loop rate, journal-ingestion silence, and corrective action are outside scope. The base SPL applies no exception lookup and makes no compliance claim.
evidence: After deployment, retain the versioned `linux_systemd_unit_failures` saved-search definition, schedule and alert history; effective Universal Forwarder `journald://systemd-start-job-failures` and `script://.../collect_systemd_failures.py` configurations; collector hash; raw `linux:systemd:unit_state` snapshots and `linux:journald:systemd` failure events; dashboard result exports; and dated positive and negative control-test outputs. Each alert row preserves `host`, `unit`, `boot_id`, source signal, `alert_key`, current state, result/exit context, first and last observation times, and a bounded journal message. Host-side `systemctl show UNIT`, `systemctl status UNIT`, and `journalctl -u UNIT --boot` captures taken before reset or restart strengthen incident evidence. These artifacts demonstrate configured collection and observed systemd state or job events; this documentation-only review did not create, sign, or runtime-validate them.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In a test index, first ingest a `sourcetype=linux:systemd:unit_state` JSON event inside the SPL's completed five-minute window with `record_type=unit_failure`, `collector_schema=1`, `collector_status=ok`, `host=systemd-positive`, `boot_id=boot-a`, `unit=uc-systemd-fail.service`, `active_state=failed`, `sub_state=failed`, `result=exit-code`, `exec_main_code=1`, `exec_main_status=42`, `state_change_timestamp=Tue 2026-07-28 18:00:00 UTC`, and `invocation_id=invocation-a`. Expect one `severity=high`, `currently_failed=1` row and a stable `alert_key` ending in `invocation-a`. Then ingest a separate `sourcetype=linux:journald:systemd` JSON event with `MESSAGE_ID=be02cf6855d2428ba40df7e9d022f03d`, `UNIT=uc-start-fail.service`, `_BOOT_ID=boot-a`, `_CURSOR=cursor-a`, and `RESULT=failed`; expect one `severity=warning`, `currently_failed=0`, `failed_start_job` row. Run with fixed event and dispatch times or shift the fixture timestamps into `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Ingest four independent controls in the same time window: a state record with `active_state=inactive`; a state record with `active_state=failed` but `collector_status=systemctl_error`; a journald event whose message merely contains "Failed" but has no matching `MESSAGE_ID`; and a journald event with the start-job failure message ID but no `UNIT`. The primary SPL must return zero rows for all four. Also ingest two repeated snapshots of the same failed unit with the same `host`, `boot_id`, `unit`, and `invocation_id`; the SPL must deduplicate them to one result row with `observation_count=1` and one stable `alert_key`. Confirm a new snapshot with a different invocation ID produces a different key so alert throttling cannot hide a later failure.

dataSources: Two complementary Universal Forwarder inputs write to the deployment-selected `index=os`. The native `[journald://systemd-start-job-failures]` input reads the local system journal with Splunk's cursor checkpoint and indexes system-manager start-job failures as `sourcetype=linux:journald:systemd`, retaining `MESSAGE_ID`, `UNIT`, `RESULT`, `JOB_ID`, `JOB_TYPE`, `PRIORITY`, `_PID`, `_UID`, `_BOOT_ID`, `_CURSOR`, and `MESSAGE`. A custom scripted input runs every 60 seconds, calls `systemctl list-units --all --state=failed` followed by machine-oriented `systemctl show` for each returned unit, and emits newline-delimited JSON as `sourcetype=linux:systemd:unit_state`. Its contract includes `record_type`, `collector_schema`, `collector_status`, `sample_epoch`, `boot_id`, `system_state`, `failed_count`, `unit`, `load_state`, `active_state`, `sub_state`, `result`, `exec_main_code`, `exec_main_status`, `n_restarts`, `state_change_timestamp`, and `invocation_id`. Splunk supplies `_time`, `host`, `source`, and `sourcetype`.
app: Splunk Universal Forwarder native journald and scripted-input capabilities, packaged in a locally managed deployment app named `TA-linux-systemd-failures`. No premium Splunk app is required. Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) can provide other host telemetry but does not define the custom unit-state event contract used here and is not a prerequisite.
spl:
index=os earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m (sourcetype="linux:systemd:unit_state" OR sourcetype="linux:journald:systemd")
| spath
| eval message_id=lower(MESSAGE_ID)
| eval signal=case(sourcetype="linux:systemd:unit_state" AND record_type="unit_failure" AND collector_schema=1 AND collector_status="ok" AND active_state="failed","current_failed_state", sourcetype="linux:journald:systemd" AND message_id="be02cf6855d2428ba40df7e9d022f03d" AND isnotnull(UNIT),"failed_start_job")
| where isnotnull(signal)
| eval unit=coalesce(unit,UNIT), boot_id=replace(coalesce(boot_id,_BOOT_ID,"unknown"),"-",""), failure_result=coalesce(result,RESULT), journal_cursor=_CURSOR, journal_message=if(signal="failed_start_job",MESSAGE,null())
| where isnotnull(host) AND isnotnull(unit)
| eval observation_identity=case(signal="current_failed_state",coalesce(invocation_id,state_change_timestamp),signal="failed_start_job",journal_cursor)
| dedup host unit boot_id signal observation_identity
| stats count AS observation_count max(eval(if(signal="current_failed_state",1,0))) AS currently_failed values(signal) AS signal_sources values(sourcetype) AS source_types latest(load_state) AS load_state latest(active_state) AS active_state latest(sub_state) AS sub_state values(failure_result) AS failure_results latest(exec_main_code) AS exec_main_code latest(exec_main_status) AS exec_main_status latest(n_restarts) AS n_restarts latest(state_change_timestamp) AS state_change_timestamp latest(invocation_id) AS invocation_id latest(journal_cursor) AS journal_cursor latest(journal_message) AS journal_message min(_time) AS first_observed max(_time) AS last_observed BY host unit boot_id
| eval failure_identity=coalesce(invocation_id,state_change_timestamp,journal_cursor,tostring(last_observed)), alert_key=host."::".unit."::".boot_id."::".failure_identity, severity=if(currently_failed=1,"high","warning"), first_observed=strftime(first_observed,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), last_observed=strftime(last_observed,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
| sort 0 -currently_failed host unit
| table severity host unit currently_failed signal_sources failure_results load_state active_state sub_state exec_main_code exec_main_status n_restarts state_change_timestamp first_observed last_observed observation_count boot_id alert_key journal_message source_types
description: Detects explicit system-level systemd failures without relying on broad log keywords. It reports units that a periodic `systemctl` snapshot observes in the high-level `failed` state and start jobs identified by systemd's structured failed-start message ID, while preserving unit, boot, state, result, exit, and journal context for triage.
value: A failed service, mount, socket, timer, or other unit can remove an application dependency while the Linux host remains reachable and its aggregate CPU or memory appears normal. State- and event-specific evidence shortens diagnosis, avoids paging on ordinary inactive units or unrelated error text, and gives platform owners a stable failure identity for routing, suppression, and post-incident review.
implementation: Deploy the native journald reader and the documented 60-second state collector from a private forwarder app, validate their exact JSON field contracts, and schedule the primary search every five minutes over the completed window. Alert when the search returns any row: page `severity=high` current failed states and route `severity=warning` failed start jobs to the owning operations queue unless local service criticality requires paging. Throttle on `alert_key` for 24 hours, not merely on host or unit, so repeated snapshots do not create duplicate pages while a later invocation can alert.
visualization: Use a latest-first table keyed by `host` and `unit` with severity, current-failure flag, signal sources, systemd result, active/sub state, exit code/status, restart counter, state-change time, last observation, and drilldown to the bounded journal message. Add single values for currently failed units and failed start jobs, plus a 24-hour trend by signal source. Place a separate collection-health panel beside it using `collection_summary` and `collection_error` records reconciled against host inventory. Do not graph repeated snapshots as failure counts or label every start-job message as a currently failed unit.
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. Native systemd journal fields and the custom systemctl state-snapshot contract do not map to a documented accelerated CIM dataset. Keep the raw-event SPL and do not claim a `tstats` equivalent.

knownFalsePositives:
The search uses explicit systemd state and message semantics, so most apparent false positives are real failures whose notification policy or attribution needs review.

1. **Intentional failure injection or resilience test** — A chaos exercise, package validation, or control test can deliberately make a disposable unit fail. Match the exact host, canonical unit, test owner, ticket, and bounded UTC interval. Preserve the event as test evidence and suppress only notification actions.

2. **Expected oneshot or maintenance helper failure** — A packaging helper, generated mount, optional device, or cleanup service may be allowed by local design to fail without customer impact. `Type=oneshot` does not itself make failure benign. Confirm the unit's contract, dependencies, `RemainAfterExit=`, exit status, and owner before adding an exception.

3. **Failed start superseded by recovery** — The structured `SD_MESSAGE_UNIT_FAILED` record reports a failed start job, not necessarily a unit that remains failed. A retry, dependency recovery, or operator action can make the unit active before the next state poll. The SPL deliberately labels this `warning` unless a current failed snapshot is also present; do not rewrite it as `current_failed_state`.

4. **Duplicate input deployment** — Two journald stanzas create two readers and duplicate journal data; two scripted stanzas repeat snapshots. The SPL deduplicates an observation identity and groups a result, but volume and evidence still become misleading. Compare `source`, `_indextime`, `_CURSOR`, deployment-app assignments, and `btool inputs list --debug`, then remove the overlap.

5. **Alias or template-instance ownership** — A failed alias can resolve to a canonical `Id`, and `worker@42.service` is operationally distinct from `worker@43.service`. Route on the canonical `unit` emitted by `systemctl show`; do not suppress every instance with a broad `worker@*` wildcard.

6. **Persistent failure snapshots** — The 60-second collector truthfully repeats a unit until it leaves `failed`. Repetition is not a new incident count. The search emits a stable `alert_key` from invocation ID or state-change timestamp; configure 24-hour field-based throttling and use `observation_count` only as collection context.

7. **Boot or clock changes** — `boot_id` separates host boots, but a bad host clock can distort `_time` and the displayed state-change timestamp. Compare `_indextime`, NTP status, boot ID, and the raw journal cursor before deciding an event is stale.

**Safe suppression:** the base SPL contains no hidden allow-list. If local policy requires one, apply an exact post-result lookup keyed by `host,unit` with required `valid_from_utc`, `valid_until_utc`, `owner`, `ticket`, `reason`, and optional expected `failure_result`. Reject wildcards and non-expiring entries; preserve suppressed rows in a review report. Never suppress solely on `failed`, `exit-code`, a host-wide key, `systemd[1]`, or an application team's unverified assertion that the service restarts.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational systemd availability monitoring; no adversary behavior is asserted)
reviewer: Cursor AI documentation-only review against primary systemd and Splunk sources; collector, journald input, control events, alert throttling, and SPL were not executed on a systemd host or Splunk platform; no SME or production validation
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and signal contract

Use a Linux host whose system service manager is systemd and install a Splunk Universal Forwarder directly in the host namespace. This UC intentionally queries the system manager only. It does not invoke `systemctl --user`, enter container or machine namespaces, or infer host state from a process list. Create a private deployment app named `TA-linux-systemd-failures`; do not edit the Universal Forwarder's system defaults or a vendor add-on's `default` directory. The forwarder service account needs permission to read the local journal and make read-only queries to systemd's system D-Bus interface. Test `journalctl --quiet --no-pager -n 1` and `systemctl show --property=SystemState` as that exact account before changing privileges. Do not grant unrestricted sudo. The Splunk search role needs read access to the selected operating-system index, permission to schedule the saved search, and access to its dashboard and alert action. No premium app is required.

Establish the measurement boundary before deployment. Systemd defines `failed` as a high-level ACTIVE state similar to inactive, except that the unit failed through an error exit, crash, timeout, too many restarts, or another unit-type-specific cause. `ActiveState` is the cross-unit state; `SubState` is finer and may change between systemd versions and unit types. `LoadState=not-found`, `masked`, or `error` describes loading, not by itself `ActiveState=failed`. `inactive` can be the expected state of a stopped service or completed oneshot. This UC therefore uses `systemctl list-units --state=failed` and verifies `ActiveState=failed` with `systemctl show`; it does not search for English words such as `Failed`, `ERROR`, or `not-found`.

The journal signal has a narrower meaning. The canonical systemd source defines `SD_MESSAGE_UNIT_FAILED` as message ID `be02cf6855d2428ba40df7e9d022f03d` and explicitly notes that the macro is misleading: it describes a failed start job, not every transition of a unit into failed state. The event commonly carries `UNIT` and `RESULT`. It can catch a short failed start even when later recovery means the next poll sees no current failure, but it cannot replace state collection. Conversely, a runtime crash that remains failed is authoritative in the state snapshot even if a distribution does not emit that start-job message. The primary search keeps `failed_start_job` and `current_failed_state` separate and raises severity only for the latter.

## Step 1 — Package and configure state and event collection

Copy `scriptExample` to `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/TA-linux-systemd-failures/bin/collect_systemd_failures.py`, make it executable, and make the app administrator its only writer. The script locates `systemctl` in `/usr/bin` or `/bin`, forces the C locale, and uses argument arrays rather than a shell. It reads `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id`, asks the manager for all currently loaded failed units, and then calls machine-oriented `systemctl show` for an exact property list. A unit that recovers between the list and show calls is counted as `race_resolved` rather than emitted as failed. Empty service-only properties remain null for other unit types. A nonzero `systemctl is-system-running` return is not treated as collection failure because `degraded` is useful manager state and intentionally returns failure; the script records stdout instead.

Configure the 60-second state input in `local/inputs.conf`:

```ini
[script://$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/TA-linux-systemd-failures/bin/collect_systemd_failures.py]
disabled = 0
interval = 60
index = os
source = linux_systemd_unit_state
sourcetype = linux:systemd:unit_state
```

A numeric scripted-input interval is seconds and the next invocation follows completion, so 60 seconds is a target cadence rather than a hard real-time guarantee. Each failed unit produces one compact JSON event per poll, followed by one `collection_summary`; a command or per-unit query error produces `collection_error`. At reference scale, a host with no failed units emits 1,440 summaries per day, while each continuously failed unit adds 1,440 events per day. Measure script duration and license volume on canaries. Never convert a collection error into `failed_count=0`, and do not use `interval=0`, which asks Splunk to restart a script continuously.

Configure JSON event breaking and search-time extraction on the appropriate parsing and search tiers:

```ini
[linux:systemd:unit_state]
SHOULD_LINEMERGE = false
LINE_BREAKER = ([\r\n]+)
TRUNCATE = 0
TIME_PREFIX = "sample_epoch"\s*:\s*
TIME_FORMAT = %s
MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD = 10
KV_MODE = json
```

The script emits one JSON object per line. Do not combine `KV_MODE=json` with `INDEXED_EXTRACTIONS=JSON`; Splunk documents that this extracts fields twice. The primary SPL also invokes `spath`, making its JSON dependency visible and easing test-index validation, but correct source-type configuration is still required for dashboards and other searches.

Add the native journald reader to the same app. Use one narrowly filtered stanza so Splunk's reader owns cursor checkpointing and resumes after restart:

```ini
[journald://systemd-start-job-failures]
disabled = 0
index = os
sourcetype = linux:journald:systemd
journalctl-include-fields = MESSAGE_ID,UNIT,RESULT,JOB_ID,JOB_TYPE,PRIORITY,_PID,_UID,_BOOT_ID,SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER
journalctl-filter = _PID=1,MESSAGE_ID=be02cf6855d2428ba40df7e9d022f03d
journalctl-quiet = true
```

Splunk's native reader always includes `MESSAGE`, `_REALTIME_TIMESTAMP`, and `_CURSOR`; the include list retains the additional contract. `_PID=1` confines this stanza to the host's system manager, and the message ID confines it to failed start jobs. Test the exact filter with the host's `journalctl` version. The Splunk documentation notes that include-field support varies on old journalctl releases. If any supported host rejects the stanza, create a separately assigned compatibility app and validate its event shape; do not silently broaden the production input to all error-priority journal data. Each journald stanza launches a reader, so duplicate stanzas duplicate records. Change `index=os` consistently in both inputs and the SPL if local index naming differs.

## Step 2 — Verify the contract, save the search, and set thresholds

Run the collector interactively as the forwarder account on a canary. In a healthy state require one `collection_summary` with `collector_status=ok`, the current `boot_id`, and zero or the same failed count shown by `systemctl list-units --all --state=failed --no-legend --plain`. For every emitted `unit_failure`, compare `unit`, `LoadState`, `ActiveState`, `SubState`, `Result`, `ExecMainCode`, `ExecMainStatus`, `NRestarts`, `StateChangeTimestamp`, and `InvocationID` with `systemctl show UNIT --all --property=...`. Require `active_state=failed`; a merely inactive unit must never appear. Some properties apply only to services, and null is correct for sockets, mounts, timers, or targets rather than zero or an invented result.

Inspect effective inputs with `$SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk btool inputs list --debug`. Search each source type over ten minutes, run `| spath`, and require the fields listed in `requiredFields` on the applicable record type. For journald, compare one safe lab start-job failure with `journalctl --boot _PID=1 MESSAGE_ID=be02cf6855d2428ba40df7e9d022f03d -o json`; confirm `UNIT`, `_BOOT_ID`, `_CURSOR`, `RESULT`, and message text survive. The first native-reader startup can log a missing-checkpoint warning because no cursor exists yet; Splunk documents this as expected first-run behavior. Subsequent cursor errors, duplicate cursors from multiple sources, or a reader that repeatedly starts from the oldest entry require correction.

Save the SPL as `linux_systemd_unit_failures` and schedule it at `*/5 * * * *`. It searches the five-minute bucket ending five minutes before dispatch (`earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m`), allowing a five-minute normal indexing delay. This is a scheduled historical search, not a real-time search. Tune the delay from measured `_time` versus `_indextime`; a source delayed beyond the allowance needs a forwarding-health fix or a deliberately larger completed window. Do not expand to 24 hours and then count repeated snapshots as new failures.

Understanding the SPL: the base search admits only the two named source types. `spath` exposes JSON fields, then `case` assigns a signal only when the complete state or message-ID predicate is true. The state branch requires schema 1, an `ok` collector, a unit-failure record, and exact `active_state=failed`. The journal branch requires the canonical lower-case message ID and `UNIT`. `coalesce` normalizes lower-case collector names and upper-case journal names without conflating their meanings. The observation identity is invocation ID or state-change timestamp for state, and cursor for journal. `dedup` removes duplicate readers or repeated snapshots of one state identity inside the bucket; it is not a substitute for removing duplicate inputs.

`stats` creates one row per host, canonical unit, and boot. `currently_failed` is one if any state observation exists; otherwise a start-job-only row stays zero. `observation_count` is the number of retained source observations, not a count of crashes, starts, users affected, or incidents. The alert key combines host, unit, boot, and the best available failure identity. Configure field-based suppression on `alert_key` for 24 hours. A repeated snapshot of one persistent failure keeps the same key, while a new service invocation, state-change timestamp, boot, or journal cursor produces a new key. Verify this behavior on your Splunk release because alert-action configuration is outside SPL.

The threshold is intentionally explicit: alert when result count is greater than zero. A current failed state is `high`; a failed start job without a current failed snapshot is `warning`. These are catalogue routing levels, not vendor thresholds. Route high to Linux/platform on-call for in-scope production hosts. Route warning to an operations queue by default, then promote exact critical units under reviewed local policy. Do not add `count>1`, `ERROR`, or a five-restarts rule to this UC; those change its semantics and belong in restart-loop or application-health monitoring.

## Step 3 — Validate positive, negative, recovery, and coverage behavior

Run both `controlTest` scenarios in a test index using fixed bounds or fixture times placed inside the completed window. Assert every output field, not just result count. The state positive must be high, preserve exit status 42, and use invocation ID in its alert key. The journal positive must remain warning and must not claim `currently_failed=1`. The inactive, collector-error, message-only, and unitless controls must produce no row. Repeated snapshots with one invocation must collapse to one host/unit/boot result and keep a stable key; a changed invocation must create a new key.

For host-side validation, create a disposable lab service, never a production dependency. One safe pattern is a transient or temporary unit whose command exits with a selected nonzero status and whose restart policy is disabled. Capture the pre-test failed list, start the unit, then promptly collect `systemctl list-units --state=failed`, `systemctl show`, `systemctl status`, and `journalctl -u` output. Confirm the state collector emits failed and the SPL reports high. Reset only the lab unit with `systemctl reset-failed UNIT`, run another poll, and confirm it no longer emits. A reset removes state evidence; retain host and Splunk captures first.

Test the event path separately with a start job that safely fails in the lab. Confirm the exact message ID exists before expecting the journal branch; distributions and failure paths can differ, and the canonical ID is specifically a failed start job. If the unit auto-recovers before a state poll, the journal-only warning is correct. If the unit remains failed, the same search row should contain both signal sources and be high. Do not force an OOM, kill a production process, corrupt a unit file, or break a shared dependency merely to satisfy monitoring.

Validate collection health independently. Reconcile expected hosts against recent `collection_summary` events; a host with no failed units must still produce summaries. Alert separately when no summary arrives for more than three target intervals or when `collector_status` is not `ok`. Compare journald reader presence in `_internal` logs and expected host inventory because the absence of failed-start events is not a heartbeat. Restart a canary forwarder, confirm the journal cursor resumes without replaying the full journal, and confirm state collection returns at the next numeric interval.

This editorial review did not execute the collector, create a failed unit, inspect a live journal, ingest fixture events, run SPL, or certify a Splunk version. `status` therefore remains `draft`, `splunkVersions` is intentionally omitted, and the reviewer metadata must not be interpreted as systemd, Splunk, Linux-distribution, or production SME approval.

## Step 4 — Operationalize response, evidence, and access

Build the visualization exactly as described and place collection health adjacent to failure results. A current-failed single value should count distinct `host,unit`, not sum snapshots. A start-job tile must say "failed start jobs" rather than "failed units." Restrict raw journal messages and unit names to platform operations and relevant service owners because command paths, internal names, arguments, and topology may be operationally sensitive. Use local retention policy; no universal audit index, CSV export, signing method, or retention period is asserted.

When an alert fires: (1) verify `host`, `unit`, `boot_id`, signal source, alert key, sample age, and raw event; (2) run `systemctl show UNIT` and `systemctl status UNIT` before changing state; (3) inspect `journalctl -u UNIT --boot` because `-u` includes messages emitted by the unit, by systemd about the unit, and related coredumps more completely than filtering only `_SYSTEMD_UNIT`; (4) decode `Result`, `ExecMainCode`, and `ExecMainStatus`, using systemd's documented exit-status tooling where needed; (5) inspect dependency failures with `systemctl list-dependencies`, resource signals, recent package/deployment/configuration changes, and application health; and (6) engage the accountable service owner before restart, reset, masking, or unit-file changes.

Do not automate `restart`, `reset-failed`, `daemon-reload`, package rollback, or configuration edits from this alert. Restart can destroy transient evidence and trigger a loop; reset-failed clears the visible failed state without correcting cause; broad daemon reloads can affect unrelated units. Preserve `systemctl show`, status, relevant journal range, current unit file and drop-ins, deployment/change identifier, and the Splunk result before remediation. After an approved fix, verify the unit reaches its intended state, the old alert key remains in history, collection summaries continue, and a deliberately new lab failure receives a new key.

Review routing inventory at least quarterly. A host-wide high alert can be noisy where hundreds of optional generated units exist. Prefer exact ownership and criticality metadata outside the base detector. Exceptions must be narrow, expiring, approved, and visible in a suppression report. A service that is "always allowed to fail" is usually a design or inventory issue; document its expected state and why an operational failure record is not actionable rather than hiding all systemd failures on the host.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot source-specific failures and suppress safely

- **No state events at all:** inspect `btool inputs list --debug`, deployment assignment, script ownership and mode, the forwarder's `ExecProcessor` messages, Python availability, and `systemctl_unavailable`/`list_units_error` records. Run both systemctl commands as the forwarder account. Do not interpret missing events as zero failed units.
- **Only summaries, despite `systemctl --failed` output:** compare the exact system-manager namespace, locale-independent `list-units --state=failed` output, per-unit `show` errors, and `race_resolved_count`. A containerized forwarder can see a different D-Bus or PID namespace and is outside this design.
- **A unit appears inactive but not failed:** that is expected. Check whether a restart or `reset-failed` occurred before the poll and inspect the journal branch. Do not broaden the predicate to all inactive units.
- **`Result` or exit fields are null:** the unit might not be a service or the property might not apply. Preserve null and use unit-type-specific properties during investigation; never turn null into success or zero.
- **No journal failure event:** verify the exact message ID with host `journalctl`, the native stanza filter, journalctl version, forwarder journal permissions, `_internal` reader errors, and cursor progress. A runtime crash is not guaranteed to emit the failed-start-job ID; current state remains the primary broad signal.
- **Journal replay or duplicates:** inspect all effective journald stanzas and their checkpoint directories. Splunk documents one reader per stanza; remove overlapping app assignments instead of relying on search deduplication.
- **Search misses late records:** compare `_time` and `_indextime`, forwarding queues, host clock, and indexer delay. Increase the completed-window delay only from measured evidence and update both schedule and test fixtures.
- **Repeated pages for one persistent failure:** verify the alert suppresses on the emitted `alert_key`, not result number, host, or unit alone. Confirm invocation ID/state timestamp stays stable and that dashboard actions are not separately paging.
- **A later failure was suppressed:** compare boot ID, invocation ID, state-change timestamp, and alert history. Reduce the throttle only after proving identities collide; do not disable deduplication globally.

If an approved test or maintenance window requires suppression, apply the exact, expiring post-result lookup described in `knownFalsePositives`. Keep the unsuppressed base result available for review and evidence. Never suppress all units on a host, every `exit-code`, all template instances, or collector errors, and never use the absence of a page as proof that the system manager, journal reader, or state collector is healthy.
grandmaExplanation: We watch when the computer's built-in service manager says an important background job could not start or has stayed broken. That helps the right team fix it before other services and users are affected.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Emit current system-manager failed units as newline-delimited JSON."""
import json
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import time

SCHEMA = 1
PATH = "/usr/bin:/bin"
PROPERTIES = (
    "Id,LoadState,ActiveState,SubState,Result,ExecMainCode,"
    "ExecMainStatus,NRestarts,StateChangeTimestamp,InvocationID"
)


def emit(**fields):
    event = {
        "collector_schema": SCHEMA,
        "sample_epoch": int(time.time()),
    }
    event.update(fields)
    print(json.dumps(event, separators=(",", ":"), sort_keys=True))


def run(systemctl, *arguments):
    return subprocess.run(
        [systemctl, *arguments],
        check=False,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        timeout=30,
        env={"PATH": PATH, "LC_ALL": "C"},
    )


def read_boot_id():
    try:
        with open("/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id", "r", encoding="ascii") as handle:
            return handle.read().strip()
    except OSError:
        return "unknown"


def parse_properties(text):
    values = {}
    for line in text.splitlines():
        key, separator, value = line.partition("=")
        if separator:
            values[key] = value
    return values


def integer_or_none(value):
    try:
        return int(value)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return None


def main():
    boot_id = read_boot_id()
    systemctl = shutil.which("systemctl", path=PATH)
    if not systemctl:
        emit(
            record_type="collection_error",
            collector_status="systemctl_unavailable",
            boot_id=boot_id,
        )
        return

    system = run(systemctl, "is-system-running")
    system_state = system.stdout.strip() or "unknown"
    listed = run(
        systemctl,
        "list-units",
        "--all",
        "--state=failed",
        "--no-legend",
        "--plain",
        "--no-pager",
    )
    if listed.returncode != 0:
        emit(
            record_type="collection_error",
            collector_status="list_units_error",
            boot_id=boot_id,
            system_state=system_state,
            error=listed.stderr.strip()[:512],
        )
        return

    units = []
    for line in listed.stdout.splitlines():
        columns = line.split()
        if columns:
            units.append(columns[0])

    emitted_failures = 0
    race_resolved = 0
    for listed_unit in units:
        shown = run(
            systemctl,
            "show",
            "--all",
            "--no-pager",
            "--property=" + PROPERTIES,
            "--",
            listed_unit,
        )
        if shown.returncode != 0:
            emit(
                record_type="collection_error",
                collector_status="show_unit_error",
                boot_id=boot_id,
                system_state=system_state,
                unit=listed_unit,
                error=shown.stderr.strip()[:512],
            )
            continue
        props = parse_properties(shown.stdout)
        if props.get("ActiveState") != "failed":
            race_resolved += 1
            continue
        emit(
            record_type="unit_failure",
            collector_status="ok",
            boot_id=boot_id,
            system_state=system_state,
            failed_count=len(units),
            unit=props.get("Id") or listed_unit,
            load_state=props.get("LoadState"),
            active_state=props.get("ActiveState"),
            sub_state=props.get("SubState"),
            result=props.get("Result") or None,
            exec_main_code=integer_or_none(props.get("ExecMainCode")),
            exec_main_status=integer_or_none(props.get("ExecMainStatus")),
            n_restarts=integer_or_none(props.get("NRestarts")),
            state_change_timestamp=props.get("StateChangeTimestamp") or None,
            invocation_id=props.get("InvocationID") or None,
        )
        emitted_failures += 1

    emit(
        record_type="collection_summary",
        collector_status="ok",
        boot_id=boot_id,
        system_state=system_state,
        failed_count=len(units),
        emitted_failure_count=emitted_failures,
        race_resolved_count=race_resolved,
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
